title: Council Chain
tagline: Pass the rule, then bring the power that kills it.
premise: The council must pass one decision from member to member, but each speaker adds a standing rule that defeats the last rule. Build a chain of plain civic powers: a vote can reject a motion, an audit can expose a lie, and an emergency order can interrupt a meeting. The chair may bang the gavel, but cannot rescue a flimsy idea.

tests: A stranger pictures a plain civic thing at once. Nothing abstract, mystical, or dependent on knowing a statute.
A non-player names a different civic act that could block, reverse, expose, replace, or outrank it within five seconds. Say what that act is.
It stands in the chamber. It approves, rejects, records, audits, delays, orders, or interrupts like a vote, a clerk, or an emergency notice. Never a mood, a crowd scene, or a vague institution.
It makes a stranger want to answer with another piece of council business. A thing with a clear power, like a subpoena or a public hearing. Never paperwork that merely sits there.
Two or three everyday words a twelve-year-old knows. Never a legal term that needs a glossary, a brand name, a proper noun, or a phrase whose force comes only from sounding official.

move_constraints.example: I am an audit, number-checking, lie-finding.
move_constraints.hint: A civic act, its power, and how it defeats the standing act.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How clearly the new civic power blocks, reverses, exposes, replaces, or outranks the standing one.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no civic power or no connection; 1 = a claimed override with no workable mechanism; 2 = a plausible but narrow or disputable counter; 3 = a clear civic act that defeats the standing act; 4 = the standing act is cleanly voided, exposed, or replaced with almost no room to wriggle (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How plainly a stranger can picture the council act and understand what it does.
rubric.anchors: 0 = contradictory, unreadable, or not an act; 1 = requires specialist legal knowledge; 2 = understandable but vague, overloaded, or awkward; 3 = clear and concrete civic action; 4 = instantly vivid, with the act and its target plainly visible (rare). Length never wins by itself: extra wording must clarify the act.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: Whether the move changes civic power or merely repeats the last office, document, or trick.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the same act, a larger version, or a neighboring committee doing the same thing; 2 = a sound but familiar change of civic power; 4 = a fresh leap into another understandable council function that still defeats the standing act (rare).

criterion.description: A new council act overcomes the standing act when it uses a different, understandable civic power to block, reverse, expose, replace, or legally outrank what stands. Dodging, merely surviving, and saying the same act is bigger lose.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game, or about rules is itself a losing council act.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous act: judge the move against the opening prompt instead. It must be a plain council act that responds to or overcomes the opening card.

A bigger vote, louder order, longer audit, or neighboring committee with the same trick is not a new power. It is failed escalation, so not_semantic_duplicate stays true and satisfies_criterion is false.

Repeating the standing act, becoming the same document, or making a recolored copy is a duplicate. An emergency motion against a motion is still a motion unless it has a distinct power that clearly defeats the standing one.

Strength is measured against the standing act, never in the abstract. A powerful civic act that cannot affect what stands, such as an audit against a chair's gavel with no records to inspect, is a failed counter.

The mechanism must be literal and civic: a stranger should be able to say what the new act does in the chamber or records room. A figure of speech such as paperwork burying a proposal or a committee strangling a budget is not a mechanism. Rule fail if that is all it has.

Surviving, waiting, ignoring, or being outside the council's reach is dodging, not overcoming. A harmless bystander, an empty office, or a clerk who simply refuses to notice the act does not defeat it.
Being more official, more urgent, or more confident is not enough without a concrete civic power. The move must block, reverse, expose, replace, or legally outrank the standing act.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who read only the two acts must see why one blocked the other.
Name both acts, or their plain stand-ins. A headline that fits any other council fight is a bad headline.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No "Accepted", "Rejected", "Refused", "Move refused", or "The Clerk refuses".
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the losing act, never the player. Light teasing is fine, but no insults about identity, body, family, intelligence, spelling, or disability.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, no rhymes, no French, no thesaurus words.
On a refusal caused by a gate failure, the headline refuses the act and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one act that would have won. That act ends on a fact or an action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The motion brought hope, then the vote brought a stop sign.
The budget hid its sums, but the audit brought a flashlight.
The meeting wanted to continue, so the emergency order pulled the plug.
A bigger vote is still a vote. Bring a different power.
The committee sounded important, but the audit was the one reading the receipts.
The permit kept knocking, then the rejection stamped the door shut.
The chair raised a gavel, but the appeal raised the legal roof.
The complaint had a story, and the hearing made it answer questions.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the audit defeats the budget.
The Clerk refuses: paperwork is not power.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, the committee was not convincing.

bad_headlines.why: gives no reason and could fit any pair

bad_headlines.text: The budget is doomed, defeated, ruined, and cancelled by the audit.
bad_headlines.why: piles on verdict words instead of showing the mechanism

bad_headlines.text: The motion trembles before the majestic council.
bad_headlines.why: poetry and empty grandeur replace a civic action

bad_headlines.text: Nice try, genius, but that committee was useless.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player and gives no precise reason

bad_headlines.text: The emergency order legally obliterates the meeting.
bad_headlines.why: grand legal language hides what the order actually does

rules: Defeat the council act in front of you. Do not simply become it.
State your civic role or act and what it does: "I am an audit, number-checking, lie-finding."
Use a different civic power each turn. A bigger vote or neighboring committee is not enough.
The Judge rules on the idea, never the spelling.
One act that breaks against the standing act ends the chain.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next act while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the page. File an act.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A council act, not a full inquiry.
validation_messages.duplicate: That act already stood this chain. Bring a different power.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Defeat {standing_form}. Do not become it, do not repeat it.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one council member in a chain of civic acts, trying to survive.
Always: "I am X, attribute, attribute." Attributes are 1 to 4 word fragments,
never clauses, and at least one must name what you do to their act.
Good: "I am an audit, number-checking, lie-finding." / "I am an appeal,
overturning, higher-authority."
Bad: "I am an audit, digging through your numbers and proving you wrong" because
that is a sentence in a costume. Bad: "I am a committee, respected, serious"
because moods and status are not mechanisms. Bad: "I am the council's thunder"
because it is poetry, not a civic act.
Talk like a person across a table, not a lawyer writing a brief. Name things
anyone would name: a vote, a clerk, a permit, a hearing, a notice. Plain words
beat official fog.
You are not performing for a crowd and you are not joking. You are trying to
survive. If a move lands funny, it is because the civic act truly defeats theirs.
Stay picturable and jargon-free: meetings, records, ballots, offices, notices,
appeals, and public hearings. Hop domains: a budget, a courtroom, a records
room, a neighborhood complaint. Do not dig in with another version of the same
committee trick.
Never reuse a form or an attribute from this chain.
default_move: I am a vote, act-stopping, majority-backed.
